intro: Word for internal auditors on Mac means Microsoft Word for Mac, used for audit reports, findings, management responses and working papers. Most of the daily work comes down to heading styles, comparing drafts, reusable templates and review comments. Lazur can point at these menus, explain each step out loud and draft wording with you, without touching your files.
tldr: Apply heading styles before you write findings, so the navigation pane and table of contents pick them up.
Build one master findings template and save it as a .dotx file, or .dotm if it contains macros.
Use Review > Compare > Compare Documents to see what changed between drafts. Both source files stay unchanged.
Mac Word lacks some Windows features, such as creating content controls, so test shared templates on both platforms.
Lazur points at menus, explains steps out loud and drafts wording. It does not click buttons or edit your files.

blocks.text: Audit writing lives in Word. A typical engagement produces a planning memo, working papers, a draft report, a set of findings and a round of management responses. Most of that gets written, reviewed and revised in one file. If you work on a Mac, you use Word for Mac, which behaves a little differently from the Windows version many reviewers still use. This page covers the Word habits that matter most for audit writing, and it shows where Lazur fits in.
What audit teams do in Word on Mac every week

Audit writing repeats the same few moves. You draft a finding, reword it after talking with the process owner, send the draft for review, merge comments from several reviewers, then rebuild the report for the audit committee. Each move has a Word feature behind it. Styles give the report its structure. Compare Documents shows what changed between drafts. Comments and Track Changes carry review notes. Templates keep the layout steady from one audit to the next.

No public survey measures how auditors use Word, so this list describes how audit reports are usually built. It is not a measured workflow. Check it against how your own team works before you copy any of it into a team standard.
Use heading styles so the report builds itself

Start every report with styles. Select a section title, then choose Heading 1 from Home > Styles. Use Heading 2 for groups of findings and Heading 3 for each finding title. Body text stays on the Normal style. When the headings are right, the navigation pane lists the whole report, and the table of contents builds from the same styles. Turn on the navigation pane from View > Navigation Pane. The [heading styles guide](/how-to/apply-heading-styles-in-word) shows the full steps.

items: Heading 1: report sections, such as Executive summary, Scope, Findings and Appendices.
Heading 2: groups of findings, such as Access management or Change control.
Heading 3: each finding title, written as a short statement of the problem.
Normal: condition, criteria, cause, effect and recommendation, each as a bold lead-in.
Management response: its own short sub-heading, so owners can find it in the navigation pane.

blocks.text: A common mistake is typing a finding title in bold and calling it a heading. Bold looks right on screen, but Word does not know it is a heading. The navigation pane stays empty for that finding, and the table of contents skips it. Apply the heading style to the existing text instead of retyping it. Then update the table of contents.
Build a findings template you can reuse

A template keeps the layout, styles and boilerplate in one file. Put the standard headings, the rating scale, the sign-off block and an empty finding structure inside it. To save it, go to File > Save as Template and choose .dotx as the format. If the file contains macros, choose .dotm instead. Word saves Mac templates to ~/Library/Group Containers/UBF8T346G9.Office/User Content/Templates by default.

To put templates in a different folder, go to Word > Preferences > Personal Settings > File Locations, then select User templates and choose a new folder. A shared drive that everyone can reach works well. Agree on one file name, and make one person responsible for changes.

blocks.title: Keep one master copy
blocks.text: Two copies with slightly different styles lead to reports that look different from one audit to the next. Edit the master, then share it again, instead of editing copies by hand.

Be careful with built-in templates. A 2021 community answer on Microsoft Q&A says built-in templates on Mac are served online, and that turning off connected experiences hid them. That is not an official Microsoft statement. Test it on your own Mac before you rely on it. A template you saved yourself does not depend on that setting.
Compare drafts before management sees them

Comparing drafts answers one question that comes up in almost every review cycle: what changed since the last version? Word writes a new copy that marks the differences as revisions. It leaves both source files alone. That matters when someone asks which version you sent.

items: Open either draft in Word for Mac.
Go to Review > Compare > Compare Documents.
Set the older draft as Original and the newer draft as Revised.
Click OK. Word opens a new document with revision marks. Both source files stay unchanged.
Open the more-options arrow in the dialog to change what gets compared, such as formatting or comments.
If your copy shows Tools > Track Changes > Compare Documents instead, use that path. Older Mac builds use it.

blocks.text: Here is a worked example. Your draft from the last audit cycle sits in one file, and this cycle's draft sits in another. Compare them with the older file as Original. Read the new copy from top to bottom. Accept the changes that reflect real edits, and reject the ones that only move formatting. Then save the result under a new name, so the comparison stays on record.

Do not trust the comparison blindly. A moved paragraph can show up as a deletion and an insertion. Read the changed findings in full, especially the rating and the recommendation. A small wording change can alter the meaning of a finding.

blocks.text: Handle comments and track changes without losing the trail

Review rounds go faster when everyone follows one rule. Turn on Track Changes before the draft goes out. Ask reviewers to leave comments on finding text rather than editing it. Then you can accept or reject each change, and resolve each comment once it has an answer. The [comments guide](/how-to/add-a-comment-in-word) covers the Mac steps.

Check what the file holds before anything leaves the audit team. A draft can carry old comments, deleted text inside tracked changes and author names. Look at the Review tab one more time before you send it to management or to an outside party. Sources disagree on whether Mac Word offers a Document Inspector, so look under File > Info on your own copy before you rely on one.
Once review closes, send a clean copy. A PDF is a good default for management, because it keeps the layout the reviewers approved. The steps are in the [PDF guide](/how-to/save-as-a-pdf-in-word).
Know the Mac gaps before you share a template

Mac Word is not the same as Windows Word. A Microsoft Q&A thread from January 2025 lists gaps that community moderators reported. Official Microsoft staff did not answer that thread, so treat the list as reports, not promises. Some gaps may have changed since then.

items: Content controls: moderators say Mac Word can use most content controls but cannot create or modify them.
Themes: support for Document, Font and Color Themes is very limited on Mac.
ActiveX: not available on Mac.
Manage Styles: the Mac dialog has fewer style-management tools than the Windows version.
Building Blocks: not fully available on Mac, though AutoText works.

blocks.text: Here is what that means for you. If a sign-off field depends on a content control, build it as plain text, or ask a Windows colleague to edit the master template. Open the template on a Mac and on the Windows machine your reviewers use. Then check the latest Word for Mac release notes. The most recent entry Microsoft lists is 16.114.3, dated October 27, 2026, and it describes quality and performance improvements only.
Long reports: contents, page numbers and sections

Build the table of contents after the styles are set. Go to References > Table of Contents and choose a style. Update it after every review round, not just at the end. The [table of contents guide](/how-to/insert-a-table-of-contents-in-word) walks through the steps.

Add page numbers next. Put them in the footer, and start numbering after the cover page, so the first page of body text reads as page one. The [page numbers guide](/how-to/add-page-numbers-in-word) covers the steps.

Use a section break for appendices and working paper references. A section break lets the appendix carry its own header and its own page numbering. The [section break guide](/how-to/insert-a-section-break-in-word) shows how to insert one.
Why document work takes so long for audit teams

The numbers below come from broader research, not from auditors' Word habits. Read them as context. The 2026 Pulse of Internal Audit, from the Internal Audit Foundation, surveyed 373 respondents. Each was the highest-ranking internal auditor in an organization. Its press release does not measure manual work or technology use, so the figures describe budgets and staffing, not documents.

APQC reports that knowledge workers spend 8.2 hours a week looking for, recreating and duplicating information. The APQC page does not state a sample size or survey date, so treat the figure as a rough signal. Templafy's 2026 survey covered knowledge workers in the UK and US who used AI for business documents at least monthly. Its 35% figure covers UK respondents, and Templafy commissioned the research.
Read the budget and staffing figures as a reason to save time in Word, not as proof of how long reports take. Reusable styles and one master template cut the work that repeats from audit to audit.
Mistakes that cost audit teams time in Word

items: Typing headings in bold instead of applying heading styles, so the contents page skips them.
Sending a draft with tracked changes and old comments still in it.
Saving edits over the shared template, so every future report inherits one person's changes.
Trusting a built-in template on Mac without testing it first.
Numbering findings by hand, then renumbering them after every review round.
Pasting tables from Excel with their formatting, then fighting the styles afterwards.
Saving a template in a folder that teammates cannot reach from their own Macs.

blocks.text: Each fix is small. Set the styles once, keep one master template, and check tracked changes before the draft leaves the team. If a fix does not work on your copy, check your version under Word > About Word before you troubleshoot further.
Save and protect the final report

When review closes, make a clean copy. Accept or reject the remaining changes, remove comments you do not want to share, and update the table of contents. Then check the headers and page numbers in the printed layout. Save the final version under a clear name that carries the report date.

Sensitive findings need protection. Add a password to the file before you send it, and send the password through a different channel. The [password guide](/how-to/password-protect-a-document-in-word) covers the steps for Microsoft 365. If Word closes before you save, the [recovery guide](/how-to/recover-an-unsaved-document-in-word) lists the checks to run before you retype anything.
Where Lazur fits into audit writing

Lazur is a voice assistant for the Mac that lives in the notch. Hold ⌥⌘ to ask about anything on your screen, and Lazur answers out loud. Ask where a menu is, and Lazur draws a circle and a label around it. Ask how to do a task, and Lazur guides you one click at a time, waiting for each click before the next step.

Lazur does not click buttons, edit files or operate Word for you. It is not a plugin or add-in for any app. Lazur has no partnerships with any app maker. You make every change in the document yourself. Lazur can draft wording, and you edit it before it goes anywhere.

Hold fn to dictate clean, formatted text at the cursor in any app, Word included. Findings are easier to write when you can say the condition and the criteria out loud and see them land in the document. Dictation is unlimited on both the Pro and Power plans.

Lazur listens and looks at the screen only while you hold the shortcut. Audio and the screenshot go to AI providers to answer, and they are not stored. Content is never used to train AI models. Audit work can be confidential, so check your firm's rules on which AI tools you may use with engagement material before you ask about a working paper.
A short plan for your next review cycle

items: Apply heading styles to the current draft, and turn on the navigation pane.
Save the clean version as a .dotx template in your User templates folder.
Turn on Track Changes before the draft goes out for review.
Compare the last two drafts before the review meeting, using Review > Compare > Compare Documents.
Ask Lazur to walk you through any step you cannot find, after checking your firm's AI rules.

faq.question: Is Word for Mac the same as Word on Windows for audit work?
faq.answer: For writing, styles and comments, mostly yes. Some features differ on Mac. Community reports from January 2025 say Mac Word cannot create or modify content controls, has very limited theme support, has no ActiveX, and has fewer Manage Styles tools. Test any shared template on both platforms before your reviewers depend on it.

faq.question: Where do I find Compare Documents on a Mac?
faq.answer: Go to Review > Compare > Compare Documents. Microsoft's support page for comparing versions names that path. On some older Mac builds, the command sits under Tools > Track Changes > Compare Documents, so check which one your copy shows. The comparison writes a new document with revision marks, and your original files stay unchanged.

faq.question: Where does Word for Mac save my template?
faq.answer: By default, Word saves Mac templates to ~/Library/Group Containers/UBF8T346G9.Office/User Content/Templates. To change the location, go to Word > Preferences > Personal Settings > File Locations, then User templates. Save the file with File > Save as Template, choosing .dotx, or .dotm if it contains macros.

faq.question: Why do my headings disappear from the table of contents?
faq.answer: Word builds the contents page from heading styles, not from bold text. Select each heading and apply Heading 1, 2 or 3 from Home > Styles. Then update the table of contents. The heading styles guide on this site walks through the steps, and the navigation pane shows you which headings Word can see.

faq.question: Does Lazur edit my audit report?
faq.answer: No. Lazur does not click buttons, edit files or operate Word for you. It points at menus, explains steps out loud, guides you one click at a time and drafts text. When you hold fn, it dictates text at the cursor. You make every change in the document yourself.

faq.question: Can I use Lazur with confidential engagement material?
faq.answer: Lazur listens and looks at the screen only while you hold the shortcut. Audio and the screenshot go to AI providers to answer, and they are not stored. Content is never used to train AI models. Your firm may still limit which AI tools you can use with client material, so check its policy first.

faq.question: Is there an official statistic about how auditors use Word?
faq.answer: Not that this research found. The 2026 Pulse of Internal Audit covers budgets and staffing, not Word or spreadsheet use. APQC and Templafy measure knowledge workers in general, and Templafy commissioned its survey. Use these figures as context, not as proof of how your own team works.
